apps.tagline: Wireless network discovery for education and authorized testing.

apps.buildNotes: The Growl notification channel is excised on this line too (SDS-10 10.6, both halves): Growl.framework no longer ships in the bundle, and scan banners post natively via NSUserNotificationCenter from the main bundle, so Notification Center attributes them to this app — its own bundle identity and icon — by construction. The self-asserted sender-identity vulnerability the inherited Growl registration created (a retired, unpatched third-party intermediary holding a user-facing trust surface) is closed estate-wide with this build: no Academy bundle ships the Growl channel any longer. The bundle stamps the SDS-10 conformance entry, including NotificationIdentity, beside the Academy audit entry.

apps.tagline: Move and resize windows with the keyboard, maintained for High Sierra.
apps.description: The Academy's maintained build of Spectacle, the keyboard-driven window manager. The inherited Sparkle 1.22/DSA update channel is replaced under the Academy Update Infrastructure Standard (Sparkle 2.9.6, EdDSA, Academy appcast) at packaging. Academy bundle identity and the Academy audit entry are verified in the shipped bundle. The app icon is cut to the amended SDS-3 construction — white tile, ink glyph, no black field; the earlier color-icon gap is closed. Current builds are signed with the Academy's self-signed code-signing identity (CN "Academy Code Signing (Self-Signed)"), so each build carries one stable designated requirement — identifier "com.detroitautomationacademy.spectacle" and certificate leaf = H"6b6f0c224d90f67ce4331368e5156f3e02ea182a" — and a macOS permission grant such as Accessibility stays attached to the app across updates instead of being asked for again on every build. Every Mach-O executable in the bundle — including Sparkle's fileop helper, which shipped with an upstream ad-hoc signature in an earlier build — is signed with that same identity, and CI deep-verifies the whole bundle (codesign --verify --deep --strict) and asserts the identity on every Mach-O before the build can publish. If Spectacle is launched from outside /Applications or from a translocated path, it names that install-location problem directly instead of showing the Accessibility prompt, because a grant cannot follow such a copy; the Accessibility check itself is unchanged for a correctly installed copy. The Accessibility dialog itself is a normal, closable window — never a modal trap: it has a working close button and its own Close button, Spectacle keeps running whether it is open or dismissed, it can be re-opened from the status-item menu while access is still missing, and it closes by itself the moment access is granted. This is not an Apple Developer ID signature and the build is not notarized. Run on the High Sierra rig: the grant-persistence verdict and the dialog retest are the owner's, at his next sitting (Distro files/46 + files/47). The bundled Sparkle updater stays at 1.22.0 in this candidate; the 2.9.6 + EdDSA step is a packaging-tranche decision.
apps.buildNotes: Dialog-trap repair build: Spectacle's Accessibility dialog is no longer a modal window you cannot put away. It opens as a normal closable window with its own Close button; closing it never quits Spectacle and never dismisses the underlying check — while access is still missing the dialog returns at the next launch and from the status-item menu, and the moment access is granted in System Preferences it closes by itself. The signing story is unchanged from the previous build — same Academy identity, same designated requirement, every executable in the bundle signed with it, whole bundle deep-verified in CI — and a copy launched from Downloads or a translocated path still gets the install-location explanation instead of the Accessibility prompt. Everything before it carries over: SDS-10 conformance (the build identifier is read from the bundle's own Info.plist at runtime and shown in the About panel and the status-item menu; the standard startup sound plays once at first presentation), LICENSE-ACADEMY.txt + NOTICE.txt bundled (Academy layer only). The owner's dialog retest and grant-persistence verdict on the High Sierra rig (Distro files/47 + files/46) are the remaining checks. Signed with a self-signed identity — not an Apple Developer ID signature, and not notarized.

The feature layer: repaired window management (no window opens partially off-screen; your window arrangement is restored), up-arrow sent-message history in the message box, markdown downloads that open in MacDown with a consented system-default offer, and a genuine Terminal view (View menu, Command-T): the app's own terminal window over the live hosted session. apps.buildNotes: Minion 0.4.4 — the menu identity fix. In 0.4.3 the application menu's Hide and Quit items carried the app's internal package identifier instead of its name: those two labels are generated from the runtime app name, and the earlier rename pass had pinned every other surface — bundle, title bar, menu title, About panel — but left those two items to the generator. 0.4.4 pins the labels in the menu itself: the items now read Hide Minion and Quit Minion. The internal identifier itself does not move — it is plumbing the sign-in machinery keys on, it is displayed nowhere else, and renaming it is what broke sign-in in 0.4.1 — so a sign-in made in an earlier build carries into this one exactly as before. Everything else stands: the 0.4.3 avatar governor (the hosted page's looping avatar animation pauses whenever the page is hidden, the window is not frontmost, or the app sits idle for 45 seconds, and resumes the moment you click, type, or a reply starts streaming; while you are working in the app the avatar animates exactly as before), bundle Minion.app under com.detroitautomationacademy.minion, Minion's own mark (the scheming side-eye dog, Academy monochrome standard), title bar pinned to Minion, dark by default (View → Appearance records your explicit choice and later launches honor it). App data is stored separately at ~/Library/Application Support/com.detroitautomationacademy.minion. Standing features: the genuine Terminal view (View menu, Command-T) over the live hosted session, markdown routing to MacDown with the consented system default, window repair, up-arrow message history, the SDS-8 welcome. Unsigned test build; the runtime verdict is the owner's, at the Air sitting.

apps.tagline: The Academy's project board — every GitHub project in one native window.
apps.description: Snowfell is the Detroit Automation Academy's Jira-style board application for Intel Macs running macOS High Sierra (10.13): every Academy project board in one native window. The bundled registry snapshot (v10-0058) carries 83 GitHub Projects boards and 763 items — the Academy's GitHub across the user smit4786 and the AutomatedTechnologies organization — with a portfolio rollup (health dot, an Open / Done split per board, and an Updated column showing each board's own GitHub updated date — the column removes itself when a snapshot carries no per-board stamps), per-board kanban whose columns are each board's own status vocabulary (data, never a hardcoded list), item detail, a roadmap over start and target dates, a command palette, an orchestration queue over a data-driven action manifest, an incidents lens for consequential matters, their evidence, and their deadlines, and the V12 Storage lens (View menu, Command-8): a multi-tenant cloud storage and content-management console over the bundled SnowfellStorageService helper, loopback-only — the service refuses any non-loopback bind unless the operator separately sets SNOWFELL_CLOUD_ALLOW_REMOTE=1 — with content-addressed deduplication by SHA-256. One window carries the navigation bar — Portfolio, Board, Staged, Orchestration, Roadmap, Incidents, Storage, Updates — and clicking a segment switches the lens in that same window: all eight lenses are visible and reachable from the one window, the filled segment always names the lens on screen, and Item Detail opens as a drill-down in the same window. No lens lives in its own window, and no segment press opens one. Every board also links back to its own GitHub Projects page: the Portfolio's GITHUB column and the Board lens each carry an “Open in GitHub” action for the board they show, opening the board's stored GitHub URL in the owner's browser. The Updates lens (Command-9) puts snapshot state on one surface: the running snapshot beside the served one, a plain line naming any gap between them, and Check Now and Apply Update as separate presses. Snapshot freshness is glanceable: the bar's Updates segment carries a filled-dot marker whenever the served snapshot differs from the running one or an update is staged, and the Portfolio header names a staged or served update in words beside the running snapshot. Changes are staged, not narrated: moving a card, adding an item, or commenting asks in plain terms — "Move '<item>' to <status> on <board>?" — and stages the change in a queue on the Mac; the full technical record (the exact GitHub operation, its destination, the staging store) sits behind each confirmation's Details button and in the Staged Changes panel, and nothing is sent without the owner's explicit Send Pending Changes in an armed build. Board state is derived, not mirrored: a board whose items all sit in its own terminal status presents as Complete (the raw GitHub state is kept as secondary detail) whenever the loaded snapshot carries the registry's derivation (schema v9+). Snowfell reads a pinned, hash-verified snapshot of the Academy registry and works fully offline; a newer snapshot can be fetched and verified in-app before it is swapped in. GitHub write-back is compiled OFF in this build (SNOWFELL_WRITEBACK_ENABLED = 0): actions stage locally and nothing is sent. Academy-original software under the Academy License (revocable). Unsigned test build. The Piles lens (design record 13, the pile organizational method) adds a ninth navigation segment: every item lives in exactly one pile — items with no Status value land in the Inbox, every board is a pile ordered by its own Status vocabulary, and the top of the selected pile is the next action — with Move to Pile, Make Top, Clear Top to the Done pile, custom piles, and within-stack drag reorder, all kept as local organizational state on the owner's Mac only. The Terminal lens (merge tranche M4) adds a tenth navigation segment and is the app's launch home: a true command-line interface to Minion over the one shared session core extracted in tranche M3 — every line enqueued first and drained head-first (FIFO, never superseded, never time-capped), with the bundled minion CLI binary at Contents/MacOS/minion as the same core's second front-end, both reporting the bundle's version from one stamped core build. The bridge's wire seam is unconfirmed until the owner's T4 wire capture (tranche M6): with no session cookie supplied a send stops at the auth boundary and nothing is sent; GUI Keychain cookie custody is M6 work and is not in this build.
apps.buildNotes: Snowfell gains the Terminal lens: the merged application's primary interface, as a tenth segment and the window's launch home. apps.tagline: On-device analytics for Academy apps — measured on the device, kept on the device.
apps.description: Tachometer is the Detroit Automation Academy's on-device analytics application for Intel Macs running macOS High Sierra (10.13). It measures the Academy's own applications where they actually run: per-process CPU and memory, itemized by role (shell, renderer, GPU, helper), so a cost like an animated avatar's is a number read off the device, not an estimate. Samples land in a segmented, append-only store under the app's own Application Support — single writer by lock, second writer refused, never merged — with rotation and retention bounds, and the built-in budget scorer reads that stream against the estate's per-app budgets (the Minion avatar budget: at most 10% of one thread sustained), reporting PASS, FAIL, or NO DATA — unmeasured is never a silent pass. There is no network code in the app: data is generated, stored, and read on the device only. Academy-original software under the Academy License (revocable). Unsigned test build.

apps.tagline: The High Sierra emulation library — verified emulator pins and a public-domain shelf, license traced per title.
apps.description: Arcadia is the Detroit Automation Academy's emulation and public-domain media library for Intel Macs running macOS High Sierra (10.13). It browses one verified catalog (schema arcadia-catalog/1; the bundled snapshot carries 74 records — 29 emulators with their last High Sierra-compatible versions pinned with evidence, 18 public-domain films, 12 homebrew games, 10 audio records, 5 television episodes — and the app refreshes from the served catalog, adopting a new snapshot only when it validates). Media is reference-only in this build (nothing is hosted yet), so no title pretends to a Play button it does not have. Academy-original software under the Academy License (revocable). apps.tagline: A client for Google Photos — the library in its own native window.
apps.description: Photos — Academy Build is the Detroit Automation Academy's native macOS client for Google Photos, for Intel Macs running macOS High Sierra (10.13). Google ships no macOS application for Google Photos; this build gives the service a window, a session, and a shelf of its own: a WKWebView on photos.google.com with a desktop Safari user agent and the persistent default website data store, so the Google session survives relaunches. Google hosts stay in the window; every other link opens in the default browser. An SDS-8 welcome shows on first launch and returns from the Help menu. Academy-original clean-room code — no Google code, no Google assets, no upstream; "Google Photos" is named only to say what the application is a client for, and the icon is the Academy's own monochrome pictogram. One risk is named plainly: Google sign-in inside embedded web views is sometimes refused ("this browser or app may not be secure"); this build's mitigations are the desktop Safari user agent, the persistent data store, and no request interception — the rig session decides whether they hold. Academy-original software under the Academy License (revocable). Unsigned test build.
apps.buildNotes: Photos — Academy Build, googlephotos-test-2 — the install fix. One honest caution, unchanged: Google sometimes refuses sign-in inside embedded web views ("this browser or app may not be secure") — if that happens here, the listing will say so and the approach re-opens. apps.tagline: One click from High Sierra to Catalina — on a new volume, High Sierra untouched.
apps.description: macOS Catalina Upgrade — MacBookAir5,2 is the Detroit Automation Academy's one-click upgrade tooling for the MacBook Air (13-inch, Mid 2012) running macOS High Sierra 10.13.6. Catalina 10.15.7 is the newest macOS Apple supports on this model (final patch Security Update 2022-005, July 2022); Big Sur drops it. Double-click Upgrade-to-Catalina.command: the first run is a dry run — model, AC power, APFS, at least 40 GB free, a Time Machine backup under 7 days old (or a typed override), and the list of 32-bit apps Catalina will not run. Type ARM and it fetches the official Catalina installer from Apple's own catalog through a pinned, hash-verified copy of installinstallmacos.py (Apache License 2.0, Greg Neagle; pin record in PIN.md), verifies Apple's signature on the installer, and installs to a NEW APFS volume named Catalina. The High Sierra volume is never overwritten — reboot holding Option to go back — because this machine class is the Academy's High Sierra rig and the dual-volume install is what keeps it one. No patcher, SIP intact. Academy-original tooling under the Academy License (revocable); the bundled fetcher is upstream open source under its own license. Unsigned test build; not yet run on the rig — the S4 verdict is the owner's.
